outcome: No event since 26 January 2024 changes the answer to the bullet as worded: the general complex-Banach question was answered negatively by Enflo (1976 outline, Acta 1987) and Read (1984 and 1985), and the Hilbert-space case that Wikipedia and the 2025 survey call open saw only claimed proofs (Enflo 2023, revised April 2024; Neville 2023; Khalil et al. 2024, refuted; Garayev 2026, withdrawn), reformulations, and a 2026 OpenAI negative result for the hyperinvariant problem, none of which I found accepted or verified.
problem_asks: One universal yes/no question: does every bounded linear operator T on every complex Banach space X send some non-trivial closed subspace M (0 is not M, and M is not X) into itself, that is T(M) inside M? Parts: (a) the quantifier over all complex Banach spaces; the statement names no dimension, separability or reflexivity restriction, so the Hilbert spaces (including separable infinite-dimensional ones) fall under the same quantifier; (b) the quantifier over all bounded operators on each such space; (c) the existence of a non-trivial closed invariant subspace. Because the claim is universal, a single complex Banach space with a single operator lacking such an M answers it no, while a yes requires a proof for every space. The Wikipedia lead's own gloss calls the problem partially unresolved, which points to the Hilbert-space restriction of part (a) as the open part; I record that restriction as a sub-case rather than as the statement.

events.what_happened: Per Enflo's Banach-space counterexample first appears as an outline in the Seminaire Maurey-Schwartz 1975-76, exposes 14 and 15, 'On the invariant subspace problem in Banach spaces' (cited there as 'to appear'). The Numdam page I opened gives bibliographic metadata only, not the exposé text. Secondary sources (Wikipedia, a 2023 history snippet not opened) say Enflo announced the result at the 1976 AMS meeting in Toronto. The full paper, per Springer metadata seen in search results (not opened), was received 10 Feb 1981, revised 21 Mar 1985 and published as Acta Math. 158 (1987) 213-313, DOI 10.1007/BF02392260.
events.revisions: Full paper received 1981 and revised 1985; journal publication 1987. Dated to the 1976 outline as the first public written argument; no earlier public written version of the full paper was found.
events.delivers: Per the 1987 Acta paper's main result as reported by Wikipedia and the 2025 survey: there is a Banach space B and a bounded operator T on B with no non-trivial closed invariant subspace. This answers the universal statement in the negative, since one counterexample suffices. Whether the space and operator are over the complex scalars is not confirmed from any text I opened; Enflo's space is described as artificial.
events.remains: Part (a) restricted to Hilbert spaces is not addressed; the counterexample lives on a non-Hilbert Banach space, per Wikipedia's statement that every known counterexample acts on a Banach space not isomorphic to a separable Hilbert space.

events.delivers: As announced: an affirmative answer for separable Hilbert spaces. Withdrawn by the authors per the Aperiodical update, so it establishes nothing.
events.remains: Everything in the claimed scope.
events.doubts: Withdrawn by the authors after a gap was found in their proof (per the Aperiodical update).

The Conversation (11 June 2023) reports that Enflo 'is reportedly cautious about the solution, as it has not yet been reviewed by experts'. events.what_happened: Sa Ge Lee, 'The Hyperinvariant Subspace Problem', arXiv 2306.13940 (single version, 24 Jun 2023). Claims the hyperinvariant subspace problem is solved for Hilbert and right Hamilton spaces, and says the work is motivated by the author's earlier invariant-subspace papers. The abstract does not claim to solve the invariant subspace problem itself.
events.delivers: As claimed: every non-scalar operator on a Hilbert (and right Hamilton) space has a non-trivial hyperinvariant subspace. This is a different question, but it bears on the invariant subspace problem by implication: a hyperinvariant subspace is invariant, so a positive answer here would also give a non-trivial invariant subspace for each non-scalar operator on those spaces. The paper does not state that consequence in the abstract I read.
events.remains: The invariant subspace problem is not claimed; the hyperinvariant case is claimed and unverified.
events.doubts: No published critique or verification found. The same author's invariant-subspace claim (2002.11533) is itself unverified.

events.what_happened: Isabelle Chalendar and Jonathan R. Partington, 'Recent perspectives on the Invariant Subspace Problem', arXiv 2507.21834 (29 Jul 2025, math.FA). Survey of about 15 years of work: almost-invariant subspaces, universal operators, classes of operators, Banach-space results. States the problem for a bounded operator on a complex Banach space of dimension at least two. Says the question was settled negatively for Banach spaces with counterexamples from Enflo and Read, that the problem 'remains open for Hilbert spaces', and that the Hilbert case 'does not seem to be solved at the time of writing'. It does not mention Enflo's 2023 Hilbert preprint, Neville, Khalil, Ghatasheh or Garayev, per my reading of its HTML. The PDF was unreadable to me, so these statements come from the HTML read through an extraction step.
events.delivers: No new result. A status survey recording that the Banach-space question has a negative answer and that the Hilbert case is open as of July 2025.
events.remains: The Hilbert case and the reflexive case, which the survey describes as open.
events.direction: No direction: a status survey.

events.what_happened: Larsen James Close, 'Chain Obstructions and Deflation in the Invariant Subspace Problem', Zenodo record 18917058 (preprint v1, published 9 Mar 2026, CC BY 4.0; ORCID given, no affiliation listed). Recasts the problem as a fixed-point problem on the lattice of closed subspaces; shows chains from the bottom and top are forced to be trivial; gives sufficient conditions for non-trivial invariant subspaces (a deflation theorem abstracting the order-theoretic part of Lomonosov's theorem, a lattice intermediate value theorem and a descending chain condition theorem). The abstract says 'All results are formalized in Lean 4 with zero sorry and zero Classical.choice'. The companion software record (Zenodo 18915083, 'witness-asymmetry', v1.0.1, 8 Mar 2026) says '93 files. 0 sorry. 0 warnings.' The Zenodo page's cross-reference DOI (10.5281/zenodo.18879768) resolves to an unrelated record, 'Point: Self-Referential Structure'.
events.delivers: Conditional sufficient conditions for non-trivial invariant subspaces, with a reformulation. The abstract describes them as sufficient conditions; it does not claim the problem is solved.
events.remains: The invariant subspace problem in general: the conditions are sufficient only.

Claims a negative answer to a question of Kim, Pearcy and Shields and 'an affirmative solution to the (hyper) invariant subspace problem in H'. Section 2 says the result 'solves the Hyperinvariant Subspace Problem'. Theorem 3.1 states that every non-scalar bounded operator on H^2 belongs to a class Delta(H^2); Corollary 3.3 states that every bounded linear operator on H^2 has a closed non-trivial invariant subspace. v2 (19 Aug 2026) is withdrawn by the author. The arXiv comments field on the abstract page reads: 'The main result of the paper, Theorem 3.1, is not correct'.
events.revisions: v2 19 Aug 2026, withdrawn by the author.
events.delivers: As claimed: an affirmative answer for the hyperinvariant problem on Hilbert space, and through it for the invariant problem on H^2 (Corollary 3.3). Withdrawn, and its comment says the main theorem is incorrect.
events.remains: Everything in the claimed scope.
events.doubts: The arXiv comments field states Theorem 3.1 is not correct; the v2 withdrawal followed. The comment's author is not identified on the page. The HTML rendering of v1 has garbled sentences in Section 1 and a repeated 'nontrivial' in Corollary 3.3.

withdrawn.what: v2 withdrawn by the author; arXiv comments: 'The main result of the paper, Theorem 3.1, is not correct'

events.direction: Affirmative (claimed) for the hyperinvariant and invariant problems on Hilbert space; withdrawn.
events.object: Claimed: every non-scalar bounded operator on H^2 lies in Delta(H^2) (Theorem 3.1), hence has a non-trivial closed invariant subspace (Corollary 3.3). The class Delta(H^2) is not described in the text I read. Withdrawn.

events.what_happened: Junsheng Fang, Bingzhe Hou, Chunlan Jiang and Yuanhang Zhang, 'The invariant subspace problem and Rosenblum operators II', arXiv 2610.11202 (v1 submitted 8 Oct 2026). Introduces an 'ideal property' for a model built from the Sobolev disk algebra and the multiplication operator. States that every intransitive operator on H is unitarily equivalent to an operator on a function algebra with this property, so 'the Invariant Subspace Problem for arbitrary operators reduces to a problem about a concrete function algebra'. Proves that certain operators with spectral radius below 1 are intransitive, with explicit invariant subspaces. Gives partial results on Pearcy's problem, rationality of generating functions, Halmos's third problem (reduced to invertible operators of a conjugate bi-geometric form) and intransitive tridiagonal operators. The paper does not claim the problem is solved.
events.delivers: A reduction of the invariant subspace problem for arbitrary operators to a problem about a concrete function algebra; intransitivity for a class of operators with spectral radius below 1; partial results on Pearcy's and Halmos's third problems. Restricted and partial; no full resolution.
events.remains: The invariant subspace problem in general, and the function-algebra problem to which it is reduced.
events.directly_checkable: The explicit intransitive operators (for example the tridiagonal examples with infinite decreasing chains of invariant subspaces) can be checked from the paper's constructions; I did not check them.
events.direction: Reduction and partial results; no answer to the invariant subspace problem.
events.object: Concrete intransitive operators: operators on the Sobolev disk algebra with spectral radius below 1 with an explicitly constructed non-trivial invariant subspace, and intransitive tridiagonal operators with infinite decreasing chains of invariant subspaces (per the abstract).

events.what_happened: GitHub issue #6048 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, 'Invariant subspace problem: prove the finite-dimensional case', opened by Konamiu on 18 Sep 2026. Closed as completed by mo271 the same day via PR #6049 (commit a2dba71, 'Prove Invariant_subspace_problem_finite_dimensional'). The Lean declaration (tagged 'research solved') says every bounded operator on a finite-dimensional complex normed space of dimension at least 2 has a non-trivial closed invariant subspace; the proof uses an eigenvector.
events.delivers: The finite-dimensional case only, which is classical (an eigenvector spans an invariant line). It bears on no part of the open infinite-dimensional problem.
events.remains: The infinite-dimensional problem, including the Hilbert and Banach cases.
events.directly_checkable: Yes: the finite-dimensional statement is a textbook fact, checkable by hand.
events.direction: Positive in the finite-dimensional case only; not a counterexample.

events.what_happened: OpenAI's preprint 'Backward intertwiners and a transitive commutant', in the openai/math repository (preprints folder dated 27 Sep 2026). I could not read the PDF: the GitHub viewer wrapper and the raw file returned no text. Its Corollary 1.2, as quoted by formal-conjectures issue #6995 (opened 8 Oct 2026): on every separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space there is a non-zero quasinilpotent bounded operator with no non-zero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace. The issue states the statement 'does not claim absence of ordinary invariant subspaces'. The openai/math README says the collection's manuscripts were 'produced by an internal OpenAI model' and that the vast majority 'were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model'. A VibeMathed page on a companion result says the manuscript is 'authored as OpenAI with no human author named' and that 'No independent mathematician has checked this yet'.
events.delivers: A negative answer to the hyperinvariant subspace problem for quasinilpotent operators on separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space (as quoted). It says nothing about ordinary invariant subspaces, and by itself it does not bear on the invariant subspace problem, since the implication runs from hyperinvariant to invariant, not the other way.
events.remains: The invariant subspace problem, which the quasinilpotent operator's invariant subspaces do not settle by this statement; the Hilbert case remains open per the survey.
events.doubts: Preprint not refereed and proof not read by me. The openai/math README warns that 'Some of the unformalized results could have issues.' The companion result on VibeMathed is labelled Lean-checked, but that label is for a different result and I did not find a Lean check of Corollary 1.2. The formalisation proposal (issue #6995, PR #7000) was open at last check.
events.direction: Negative answer to the hyperinvariant problem for quasinilpotent operators, per the quoted corollary; not a statement about the invariant subspace problem.
events.object: A non-zero quasinilpotent bounded operator on every separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space with no non-zero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace (Corollary 1.2 as quoted). Whether the operator is explicit or from an existence argument was not established from the sources I could read.

The README is repository-wide: it does not name this preprint or its corollary, and the preprint's own production statement was not readable to me.
systems.basis_quote: The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model.

ai.disclosed_cost: Per the openai/math README as extracted: each result used roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking compute, and the model was posed about 4,000 problems. This is a repository-wide statement, not specific to this corollary, and the quotation is from a model-extracted summary of the page.

events.what_happened: GitHub issue #6995 in google-deepmind/formal-conjectures, 'Add a quasinilpotent operator without a hyperinvariant subspace', opened 8 Oct 2026 by anxkhn. It proposes a Lean formalisation of Corollary 1.2 of the OpenAI preprint; linked PR #7000 was open at last check. The proposer reports a scoped '--wfail' check and a separate statement review passed, and 'no external formal_proof claim is proposed'. The body names no AI system or model.
events.delivers: A formal statement proposal for the hyperinvariant corollary. It establishes nothing by itself and is not about the invariant subspace problem.
events.remains: The invariant subspace problem, entirely.
events.direction: Not the invariant subspace problem.

events.what_happened: Repository zblore/fc-isp-normal, single commit dated 10 Oct 2026, 'Prove the invariant subspace problem for normal operators against Formal Conjectures'. Its README says the repo is a Lean 4 proof that every normal operator on a complex Hilbert space of dimension at least two has a non-trivial closed invariant subspace, against the formal-conjectures declaration Invariant_subspace_problem_normal_operator. The README says 'I used Claude Code to draft the Lean.' It says the proof uses only propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and does not state a sorry count. The README also says a GitHub user 'baobingzhang' proved the same statement in Lean in September 2026 as part of a Lomonosov formalisation; I did not open that repository.
events.delivers: A formal proof for normal operators, a classical restricted class with an elementary proof via the spectral theorem. It bears on no part of the open problem beyond that class.
events.remains: Every non-normal operator, and the general problem.
events.directly_checkable: Yes: the normal-operator statement is classical and checkable by hand from the spectral theorem.
events.direction: Positive for normal operators only; not a counterexample.

disputes.summary: Khalil et al. (Axioms, Sept 2024) claim the separable Hilbert case; Ghatasheh (arXiv Nov 2024, v2 Mar 2025) says the argument is incorrect, identifying a 'Fourth Claim' with an ill-defined functional. An automated Pith referee (12 Aug 2026) judged the refutation 'mathematically right in essence' but said its own Theorem 1.13 needs a fix. The journal investigation is reported only from search text.
Enflo (arXiv 24 May 2023) and Neville (arXiv 17 Jul 2023) both claim the separable Hilbert case. Neville's introduction acknowledges Enflo's earlier posting and builds on his own 2022 preprint.

Garayev's withdrawn July 2026 claim (every non-scalar bounded operator on H^2 lies in Delta(H^2)) and the OpenAI September 2026 corollary (a non-zero quasinilpotent operator on separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space with no non-zero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace), as quoted by the formal-conjectures issue, cannot both hold for H^2 as stated. Garayev's version is withdrawn with a comment that Theorem 3.1 is incorrect; the OpenAI corollary is unrefereed and I did not read its proof. Both concern the hyperinvariant problem, not the invariant problem directly.

Earlier claims withdrawn by their authors: Cowen and Gallardo (Jan 2013; withdrawn Feb 2013 for a gap); Garayev (Oct 2013; withdrawn Nov 2013 for a gap in Claim 1); Kerchy and Pearcy (Mar 2025; withdrawn Mar 2025 after a counterexample to Theorem 3 reported by Bercovici); Garayev (Jul 2026; withdrawn Aug 2026). Lee's invariant-subspace claim (Feb 2020 onward) carries a withdrawn v3 with no stated reason and no published verification.

summary: Nothing in the window changes the answer to the bullet as worded. The universal question (every bounded operator on every complex Banach space has a non-trivial closed invariant subspace) was answered negatively by Enflo (the 1975-76 Seminaire outline, Acta Math. 1987) and by Read (1984 and 1985, on l1 and related spaces). The Chalendar-Partington survey (July 2025) and the formal-conjectures Lean file both record this. Whether those counterexamples are over the complex scalars is not confirmed from any text I opened; the Lean file takes l1 over C, but its body is sorry. The Hilbert-space case, which Wikipedia's lead and the survey call open, is the part where new events fall. The in-window claims there are: Enflo's preprint (v1 24 May 2023, v2 6 Apr 2024 with the claim unchanged; no referee report, journal reference or expert check found; the July 2025 survey does not mention it); Neville (17 Jul 2023, separable case, citing Enflo; no review found); Lee (Feb 2020 onward, 'solved', with Theorem 2.1 for separable Hilbert spaces; a withdrawn v3; no review found); Khalil et al. (Axioms, Sept 2024, refuted by Ghatasheh in Nov 2024, whose argument identifies the Fourth Claim as ill-defined; the journal investigation is only reported in search text, since MDPI and DOAJ returned 403); and Garayev (17 Jul 2026, H^2 and hyperinvariant, withdrawn 19 Aug 2026 with the comment that Theorem 3.1 is not correct). Foukzon (2022, non-standard analysis, PhilArchive only, 403 on fetch) has no engagement found. Reformulations and partial results: Fang, Hou, Jiang and Zhang I (June 2025) and II (8 Oct 2026, a reduction to a function-algebra problem); Close (March 2026, conditional sufficient conditions, with a Lean companion that claims zero sorry and a DOI cross-reference that resolves to an unrelated paper); Kerchy and Pearcy (March 2025, a claimed equivalence with the hyperinvariant problem, withdrawn). An important logical point for the judging pass: a hyperinvariant subspace is invariant, so a positive answer to the hyperinvariant problem on Hilbert space would also give invariant subspaces there. That is why Lee's 2023 hyperinvariant claim and Garayev's 2026 claim bear on the Hilbert case by implication, although neither abstract draws the consequence in the same words as the invariant-problem claim. The reverse does not hold: the OpenAI corollary (27 Sep 2026, quoted in formal-conjectures issue #6995) is a negative answer to the hyperinvariant problem for quasinilpotent operators, and by its own statement it does not decide ordinary invariant subspaces. AI involvement: none of the sources bearing on the invariant-subspace claims names an AI system. Enflo, Neville, Lee, Khalil, Ghatasheh, Garayev, Fang I and II, Close, Kerchy, Szczepanski and the survey all have no AI or software statement on the pages I read, and the full-text checks listed in incomplete cover most but not all of them. AI appears in three other places. (i) OpenAI's hyperinvariant corollary: the openai/math README says the collection was 'produced by an internal OpenAI model' and 'obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model'; that is repository-wide, and I could not read the preprint itself. (ii) The zblore normal-operator Lean (10 Oct 2026): 'I used Claude Code to draft the Lean.' This formalises a classical special case, so under section 5.4 it is recorded as involvement without an entry in ai.systems. (iii) The Pith review of Ghatasheh is an AI referee, not a contribution to the mathematics. Three leads were checked and not recorded as AI involvement. A ProofAtlas search snippet said the problem was 'source-reported proved', citing an OpenAI release of 6 Oct 2026; the ProofAtlas entry I read (entry 106, 'Invariant Subspace Problem for Hilbert Space Operators') is labelled 'Open', with no lab attribution, and the snippet's own statement mismatched the Iitaka conjecture, so I treat the snippet as wrong. A search snippet describing an 'AI-assisted' Lean formalisation of Lomonosov's theorem in plby/lean-proofs was checked and is an Erdos 603 registration unrelated to this problem. A Lean repository described as covering normal operators is recorded as event zblore-normal-operators-2026. The formal-conjectures file states the bullet as the separable Hilbert case (research open, body sorry), not as the complex Banach case; that narrowing is the file's choice, and I record it here so the judging pass can see it. On the denominator question, the record is not a 'nothing happened' case: there are many events, all of them about the Hilbert case or about restricted classes, and the general question was already decided before the window.
competing_reading: The bullet names the universal question, which was answered negatively in 1985, so every in-window event is about a different question (the Hilbert case, or hyperinvariant or restricted classes), and the status of the bullet is unchanged since 2024. The opposite reading takes the bullet's own gloss, that the problem is partially unresolved, to mean the Hilbert case is the intended open problem. On that reading the in-window claims matter: Enflo 2023 (v2 Apr 2024) and Neville 2023 would settle it if correct; Khalil et al. would have settled it, but the refutation stands against them; Garayev 2026 is withdrawn. On either reading, the judging pass should separate the claims that are withdrawn or refuted from those that are unverified but standing, which are Enflo 2023, Neville 2023, Lee 2020 and Lee 2023 (hyperinvariant).
what_would_settle_it: For the universal question: the complex scalar field of Enflo's 1987 space and of Read's 1984 and 1985 operators, from the Acta and Bull LMS texts. For the Hilbert case: a journal decision on Enflo 2023 (its arXiv journal-reference field, MathSciNet or zbMATH), a published expert verification or refutation of Enflo 2023 and Neville 2023, a Lean formalisation of either argument without sorry, and the outcome of the Axioms investigation into Khalil et al. (the MDPI record, not readable to me). For the hyperinvariant link: the OpenAI preprint's full text and its production statement, and any refereeing of Corollary 1.2. For Lee 2002.11533: a journal version, or a published critique. For AI: an author statement that names a system for any of the Hilbert-case claims. None of these appeared in the sources I could read.
